title: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091  Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092  Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator. F093  Nanorobotic Collective Pheromone Communication At The Limit — Explores prospective chemical-trail or signal-mediated coordination with collision exposure as a primary outcome. Hidden actuator saturation and a matched-actuation single-agent baseline challenge claims that signaling, rather than redundancy or imposed motion, caused the improvement. F094  Microscale Robot Collective Collision Avoidance Control At The Limit — Examines collision-safe motion while monitoring spatial coverage, recovery time and communication burden. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether apparent avoidance depends on erroneous common position estimates; safety-boundary crossings trigger rejection. F095  Nanorobotic Collective Energy Allocation At The Limit — Tests dynamic allocation of limited energy across agents during dropout and recovery. Hidden agent-loss clusters challenge energy accounting and recovery-time claims against fixed rules with an equal energy budget; persistent unsafe confidence is a stop condition. F096  Microrobotic Distributed Mission Planning At The Limit — Studies task planning without a central controller using communication load, work-per-task and selective abstention as prospective metrics. Hidden network partitions expose plans that depend on unavailable messages, while a matched-actuation single-agent system tests whether coordination adds value. F097  Nanorobotic Collective Localization Uncertainty At The Limit — Tests whether robots can act safely when position confidence is uncertain or neighbors provide deceptive state information. Energy per accepted task, abstention and completion are checked against a full-state centralized benchmark; unrecognized safety-boundary crossings invalidate the claim. F098  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Topology Control At The Limit — Examines when changing neighbor connections should trigger reconfiguration or justified refusal to proceed. Hidden actuator saturation challenges topology decisions; fixed energy-matched rules and independent task and consensus measurements distinguish adaptive control from misleading internal agreement. F099  Nanorobotic Collective Fault Isolation At The Limit — Investigates recognition and containment of malfunctioning agents without allowing errors to propagate across the swarm. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether fault labels confuse a common sensor defect with separate robot failures; recovery to a known-safe state is mandatory. F100  Microrobotic Collective Mission Handoff At The Limit — Designs a traceable transfer of task state and authority across agents after concealed dropout clusters. The study checks consensus error, collisions and coverage against centralized full-state control; an apparently successful handoff is rejected if safety invariants are violated. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten volumes are prospective, nonclinical research-design working editions for traceable materials, authorized ex-vivo systems, synthetic phantoms and bench-scale microfluidic tests. Proposed comparisons require preregistered budgets, blinded perturbations, independent reference measurements, complete negative-trial denominators and explicit safety stops. No new experimental results, validated in-body autonomy or clinical benefit are claimed. Mathematical derivations, physical unit consistency, claim-level DOI linkage and substantive causal novelty still require specialist review; the automatic Gate-text distinctness audit cannot replace it. They are reference points for existing methods, not evidence that any STARLI-specific candidate device or proposed experimental advantage has been demonstrated. Independent source-to-claim verification remains necessary. A single-agent controller with matched total actuation tests whether the apparent gain comes merely from redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state ends the trial. F103  Nanorobotic Collective Safe Stop At The Limit — Defines a test of independently observed transition to a safe state after a collective disturbance. The witness is time to demonstrably safe state [s], preserving the atlas recovery-time field. A fully observing centralized controller provides the comparator; increased agent count is an alternative cause of faster recovery. Crossing any registered safety invariant terminates evaluation. F104  Microrobotic Collective Local Sensor Fusion At The Limit — Examines whether local sensor exchange improves accepted mission decisions under limited communication. Communication traffic per accepted task [bytes/task] is a proposed measurement, with the original communication-load outcome retained. Equal-energy fixed rules challenge the fusion benefit; unacknowledged global state tracking is a competing explanation. Hidden partitions test whether confidence remains appropriately bounded. F105  Nanorobotic Collective Asynchronous Control At The Limit — Investigates decision timing when individual robots update at different rates rather than using a single synchronized command. Total metered energy per completed task [J/task] is the proposed observable, preserving the atlas energy-per-task field. The control comparison matches total actuation to a single-agent system; redundancy without true adaptation is the alternative. Failure to regain a known-safe state requires stopping. F106  Microrobotic Collective Task Competition And Coordination At The Limit — Proposes experiments in which agents must choose between competing tasks under bounded control authority. Selective abstention and service coverage [fraction] is the candidate measurement, anchored to the atlas abstention outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the strong comparator, with simple agent-number advantage as a rival. Breach of registered safety invariants invalidates any coordination gain. F107  Nanorobotic Collective Adaptive Path Planning At The Limit — Tests whether locally coordinated route changes improve mission completion when obstacles or task geometry vary. Task-success fraction under equal energy [fraction] is the proposed endpoint, linked to the original task-completion measure. Fixed behavior at the same energy budget is the baseline; leaked external tracking may falsely suggest adaptation. Concealed network partitions probe erroneous collective confidence. F108  Microrobotic Collective Contamination Control At The Limit — Addresses a different physical constraint: preserving sample separation during repeated collective handling. The new proposed endpoint is cross-sample chemical carryover [mass fraction], while the source atlas retains consensus error. A matched-actuation single-agent control tests claimed collective benefit; redundancy alone may explain task performance. Inability to return to a known-safe state is a mandatory stop. F109  Nanorobotic Collective Collaboration Reliability At The Limit — Examines whether distributed cooperation can remain safe and reproducible across adverse trials. Hazardful collision frequency [events/(agent*min)] is the candidate observable alongside the original collision-rate outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the baseline, and additional robots are a rival source of apparent performance. Safety-invariant crossing overrides aggregate success statistics. F110  Microrobotic Collective Heterogeneous Agents Coordination At The Limit — Studies coordination across agents with different sensing, mobility or task roles, while preserving traceable collective outcomes. Coverage entropy under heterogeneous roles [nat] is the proposed witness. Equal-energy fixed behavior is the baseline; outside tracking that silently supplies global state is a competing explanation. Unjustified high confidence during a concealed partition rejects the proposal. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These are prospective nonclinical research designs restricted to authorized bench-scale, ex-vivo or synthetic reference settings with traceable sample identity, calibrated measurement and bounded actuation. Proposed endpoints are editorial additions and do not replace original atlas outcomes. No laboratory experiments or clinical results are reported. Matched energy and actuation, blinded disturbances, full negative-trial records and noncompensable safety stops are needed before any advantage claim. title: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091  Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092  Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator. F093  Nanorobotic Collective Pheromone Communication At The Limit — Explores prospective chemical-trail or signal-mediated coordination with collision exposure as a primary outcome. Hidden actuator saturation and a matched-actuation single-agent baseline challenge claims that signaling, rather than redundancy or imposed motion, caused the improvement. F094  Microscale Robot Collective Collision Avoidance Control At The Limit — Examines collision-safe motion while monitoring spatial coverage, recovery time and communication burden. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether apparent avoidance depends on erroneous common position estimates; safety-boundary crossings trigger rejection. F095  Nanorobotic Collective Energy Allocation At The Limit — Tests dynamic allocation of limited energy across agents during dropout and recovery. Hidden agent-loss clusters challenge energy accounting and recovery-time claims against fixed rules with an equal energy budget; persistent unsafe confidence is a stop condition. F096  Microrobotic Distributed Mission Planning At The Limit — Studies task planning without a central controller using communication load, work-per-task and selective abstention as prospective metrics. Hidden network partitions expose plans that depend on unavailable messages, while a matched-actuation single-agent system tests whether coordination adds value. F097  Nanorobotic Collective Localization Uncertainty At The Limit — Tests whether robots can act safely when position confidence is uncertain or neighbors provide deceptive state information. Energy per accepted task, abstention and completion are checked against a full-state centralized benchmark; unrecognized safety-boundary crossings invalidate the claim. F098  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Topology Control At The Limit — Examines when changing neighbor connections should trigger reconfiguration or justified refusal to proceed. Hidden actuator saturation challenges topology decisions; fixed energy-matched rules and independent task and consensus measurements distinguish adaptive control from misleading internal agreement. F099  Nanorobotic Collective Fault Isolation At The Limit — Investigates recognition and containment of malfunctioning agents without allowing errors to propagate across the swarm. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether fault labels confuse a common sensor defect with separate robot failures; recovery to a known-safe state is mandatory. F100  Microrobotic Collective Mission Handoff At The Limit — Designs a traceable transfer of task state and authority across agents after concealed dropout clusters. The study checks consensus error, collisions and coverage against centralized full-state control; an apparently successful handoff is rejected if safety invariants are violated. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten volumes are prospective, nonclinical research-design working editions for traceable materials, authorized ex-vivo systems, synthetic phantoms and bench-scale microfluidic tests. Proposed comparisons require preregistered budgets, blinded perturbations, independent reference measurements, complete negative-trial denominators and explicit safety stops. No new experimental results, validated in-body autonomy or clinical benefit are claimed. Mathematical derivations, physical unit consistency, claim-level DOI linkage and substantive causal novelty still require specialist review; the automatic Gate-text distinctness audit cannot replace it. title: METASURFACE-GUIDED MICROROBOTIC CONTROL AT THE LIMIT STARLI | Institute XXIV | Flagship 14 of 30 | Research Group B This prospective research monograph asks when phase-gradient metasurfaces can become reliable optical-control infrastructure for microscopic agents rather than merely generating visually persuasive multifocal wavefronts. Its central research coupling combines metasurface phase-gradient engineering, independently verified optical-field and force shaping, and robust multi-agent positioning under realistic manufacturing, polarization, thermal and task constraints. The investigation follows a falsifiable route from vector electromagnetic interface models and fabricated nanoantenna tolerances to calibrated force and thermofluid attribution, Brownian particle motion, multi-agent collision risk, optical tracking, safe control fallback and cross-batch replication. Ghost foci and polarization drift are treated as testable safety hazards. The strongest conventional benchmarks are optimized spatial light modulators and matched microlens arrays evaluated at equal delivered optical dose, throughput, tracking quality and thermal limits. A metasurface is judged by independently confirmed task completion, not by diffraction efficiency or wavefront quality alone. The manuscript is structured as 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. External DOI literature, a four-monograph intellectual lineage and a companion Excel evidence atlas support traceable source navigation and successor-led experiments. The monograph retains negative-result routes: if classical optics provide equal control with lower total risk or cost, that is a meaningful scientific conclusion. The work does not assert a verified autonomous microrobot, a demonstrated multi-agent industrial controller, or a discovered physical law. It is a research architecture that proposes mechanisms, prospective tests, alternative explanations, independent measurements and stopping criteria. Literature from atom trapping, integrated phased arrays and optical force inverse design is explicitly treated as contextual evidence rather than a demonstration of fluidic microrobot autonomy.

title: CONCEPTUAL EMERGENCE & GENERATIVE INTELLIGENCE AT THE LIMIT Living Concept Civilization — Flagship Research Monograph 06 STARLI / White Rainbow Civilization · October 2026  ABSTRACT  When do interactions among concepts, models, tools and people produce a genuinely new, independently verifiable capacity rather than a novel label or a misleading evaluation threshold? This English-language research monograph develops a falsifiable program for conceptual emergence and generative intelligence. Its research three-coupling is Interaction Generation × New-Function Identification × Counterfactual Verification. The proposed emergence expression compares held-out capability improvement with the strongest viable baseline and a contamination penalty, with all terms requiring operational definition and appropriate normalization before use.  RESEARCH DESIGN  The volume studies both smooth scaling and possible discontinuities, evaluation-metric sensitivity, training-data leakage, compositional generalization, simple-rule baselines, factorial component ablation, multi-agent collaboration, correlated errors, human-AI complementarity, multimodal grounding, causal interventions, tool-dependence, calibration, cross-model reproducibility, governance, and intergenerational handoff. A claimed capability must survive preregistered unseen tasks, strong comparators, counterfactual perturbations and independent reproduction. A fluent explanation, a generated new term or a model's assertion of consciousness is not evidence of functional emergence.  MONOGRAPH STRUCTURE  The 82 research chapters each present one distinct proposed chapter-wide operational equation, followed by twelve independently paginated study sections. Thirty advanced physics derivation routes appear in the preface with three-dimensional conceptual diagrams; they are existing physics statements within specified domains and do not establish laws of language or awareness. The concluding 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos each feature one of 233 distinct physical equation anchors. These equations are methodological contrasts and educational prompts, not proof of the emergence hypotheses. A separate Excel workbook indexes chapters, sections, gates, candidate mechanisms and physics anchors.  EVIDENCE AND ETHICS  This monograph is a theoretical and experimental research agenda. It reports no new trials, controlled effects or validated discoveries; all proposed mechanisms, metrics, forecasts and outcomes are UNVERIFIED until independently tested. The distinction between appearance under a chosen test and a robust new function must be maintained. Consent, intellectual provenance, lawful data use, security and affected persons' right to refuse are hard constraints rather than offsettable penalties.  OPEN RESEARCH INVITATION  Research Gates reserve space for questions that can be rejected, refined or answered by future researchers. Phoenix Answer Embryos are provisional designs that can be falsified, decomposed, recombined or responsibly retired. The goal is not a permanent claim that machines awaken or that thought obeys physical equations; it is an enduring, contestable toolkit for recognizing and scrutinizing useful new functions.  FOUNDATIONS  Project source: Living Concept Civilization — Eighteen Tri-Coupled Flagship Research Programs, v2.0 (2026-10-13), Flagship 06. (2023), https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.15004. Chollet, On the Measure of Intelligence (2019), https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.01547.
